3.8 Financial Ratios

Profitability and the DuPont decomposition

Section titled “Profitability and the DuPont decomposition”

The statements in 3.7 Financial Statement Analysis give amounts. Amounts depend on the size of the company, so to compare different companies, or one company across years, we use ratios. This lesson writes SSS for revenue, NI\text{NI}NI for net income, AAA for total assets, EEE for shareholders’ equity and DDD for interest-bearing debt.

Ratios that measure profitability include:

  • gross margin, operating margin and net margin: gross profit, operating income (EBIT) and net income, each divided by revenue;
  • return on assets (ROA): NIA\frac{\text{NI}}{A}ANI​, how much profit the assets earn;
  • return on equity (ROE): NIE\frac{\text{NI}}{E}ENI​, the return on the book capital shareholders have put in.

ROE is one of the ratios shareholders care about most. It can be split into the product of three ratios:

ROE=NIS×SA×AE\text{ROE} = \frac{\text{NI}}{S} \times \frac{S}{A} \times \frac{A}{E}ROE=SNI​×AS​×EA​

The three terms are the net margin, asset turnover (how much revenue each dollar of assets brings in) and the equity multiplier (how many dollars of assets each dollar of equity supports). This is DuPont analysis. It shows that ROE can come from three different sources: selling at a high price (high margin), selling a lot (high turnover), or borrowing a lot (high leverage). Supermarkets have very low margins and rely on high turnover; software companies have very high margins and lower turnover; banks have neither high margins nor high turnover and rely on very high leverage. The same ROE from different sources carries different risk and may last differently.

Check C1
Companies A and B both have an ROE of 20%. A: net margin 20%, asset turnover 0.5, equity multiplier 2. B: net margin 2%, asset turnover 2.5, equity multiplier 4. If both companies' revenue falls 10% and their costs cannot fall in proportion, whose ROE is more likely to fall sharply?
A high margin gives a large cushion when revenue falls, so profit does not easily turn negative.
The ROEs are equal but come from different sources: look at each company's margin and leverage.
High asset turnover does not add risk by itself. Think about what a 10% fall in revenue does with a 2% margin.

Financial leverage

Section titled “Financial leverage”

Financing assets with debt is financial leverage. To see what it does, ignore taxes for now and read ROA as profit before interest divided by total assets. Assets are A=D+EA = D + EA=D+E and interest is rDrDrD, so the profit left for shareholders is ROA×A−rD\text{ROA} \times A - rDROA×A−rD; dividing by EEE:

ROE=ROA+(ROA−r)DE\text{ROE} = \text{ROA} + (\text{ROA} - r)\frac{D}{E}ROE=ROA+(ROA−r)ED​
Check C2
In Figure 2-1, set debt/equity to 2 and the interest rate to 5%. When the return on assets falls from 10% to 2%, the ROE of the company with debt:
With debt, fixed interest must still be paid. When the return on assets is below the interest rate, interest takes a larger share.
Debt raises ROE only when the return on assets exceeds the interest rate. Here the return on assets falls to 2% and the rate is 5%.
The debt ratio is unchanged, but the return on assets changed, so ROE changes too, magnified by leverage.

Efficiency and return on capital

Section titled “Efficiency and return on capital”

Ratios that measure efficiency include:

  • asset turnover: revenue ÷ total assets;
  • days of receivables (DSO): receivables ÷ revenue × 365;
  • days of inventory (DIO): inventory ÷ cost of goods sold × 365;
  • days of payables (DPO): payables ÷ cost of goods sold × 365.

Together they give the cash conversion cycle: DSO + DIO − DPO, the average number of days from paying for materials to collecting from customers. The longer the cycle, the more money is tied up in working capital.

ROE and ROA both depend on financing: ROE changes with leverage, and ROA deducts interest in the numerator while including assets bought with debt in the denominator. To measure the return of the business itself, a common ratio is return on invested capital (ROIC):

ROIC=EBIT (1−t)D+E\text{ROIC} = \frac{\text{EBIT}\,(1 - t)}{D + E}ROIC=D+EEBIT(1−t)​

The numerator is after-tax operating profit regardless of financing, the denominator is the capital supplied by shareholders and creditors, and ttt is the tax rate. ROIC should be compared with the return investors require on this capital, the cost of capital, in the same spirit as economic profit. Is expansion good for a company whose ROIC is below its cost of capital? Check C3

Check C3
A company's ROIC is 6% and its cost of capital 9%, and neither is expected to change. It plans to invest more capital to expand, which will raise both revenue and profit. For shareholders, this expansion is:
Growth in accounting profit is not growth in value. How does the return on new investment compare with what investors require?
ROIC is unchanged, but the new capital still earns only 6%. What do investors require on it?
Becoming larger does not make up for earning less than the cost of capital.

Solvency and liquidity

Section titled “Solvency and liquidity”

Creditors care more about whether the company can pay on time:

  • leverage ratios: debt ÷ equity, debt ÷ total assets, interest-bearing debt ÷ EBITDA (EBITDA is operating income plus depreciation and amortization, a rough measure of cash generated by operations);
  • interest coverage: EBIT ÷ interest expense, how many times operating income covers interest;
  • current ratio: current assets ÷ current liabilities; quick ratio: (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities. Current assets and current liabilities are items that will turn into cash or must be paid within a year.

Rating agencies (3.6 Credit Risk) pay close attention to leverage ratios and interest coverage.

Check C4
An electric utility and a semiconductor company have the same debt ÷ equity and, for now, the same interest coverage. Which is riskier for creditors?
The amount of assets does not decide debt risk. What matters is how far profit and cash flow can fall in bad years.
The ratios describe only the present. In a recession, would both companies' profits change by the same amount?
Creditors care about being paid interest and principal on time, which depends mainly on profit and cash flow, not on the share price.

Cautions in using ratios

Section titled “Cautions in using ratios”
  • Compare within the same industry, and look at a company’s own trend over time; “normal” ratios differ a lot across industries.
  • Ratios inherit the problems of accounting numbers (3.7 Financial Statement Analysis): one-time items, accounting estimates and differences in accounting policies all affect them.
  • Large share buybacks reduce equity and raise ROE and the equity multiplier, and can even make book equity negative, in which case ROE loses its meaning.
  • Changes in accounting rules change ratios: for example, from fiscal year 2019 US public companies put most operating leases on the balance sheet under the new lease standard (ASC 842), noticeably raising assets and liabilities in lease-heavy industries such as retail and airlines.
  • Ratios describe the past; valuation is about the future (3.9 Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models).

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • ROA =NIA= \frac{\text{NI}}{A}=ANI​, ROE =NIE= \frac{\text{NI}}{E}=ENI​; DuPont analysis: ROE = net margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier.
  • Ignoring taxes, ROE=ROA+(ROA−r)DE\text{ROE} = \text{ROA} + (\text{ROA} - r)\frac{D}{E}ROE=ROA+(ROA−r)ED​: leverage makes ROE more sensitive to ROA.
  • Efficiency: turnover, days of receivables, days of inventory, days of payables and the cash conversion cycle. ROIC =EBIT(1−t)D+E= \frac{\text{EBIT}(1 - t)}{D + E}=D+EEBIT(1−t)​ does not depend on financing and should be compared with the cost of capital.
  • Solvency and liquidity: debt ratios, interest-bearing debt ÷ EBITDA, interest coverage, the current ratio and the quick ratio.
  • Compare ratios within an industry and over time, and watch for the effects of accounting numbers, buybacks and changes in accounting rules.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1 ★
A company in year 1: net income 100, revenue 1000, total assets 1000, equity 500. In year 2 it borrowed to buy back some shares: net income 95 (higher interest), revenue 1000, total assets 1000, equity 380.
(a) Decompose ROE in both years with DuPont analysis.
(b) Does the change in ROE show that the business improved? How should shareholders view the buyback?
Question 2
A company has an ROIC of 7%, an after-tax cost of debt of 4%, and debt ÷ equity of 2.5. One can show that ROE=ROIC+(ROIC−rd)DE\text{ROE} = \text{ROIC} + (\text{ROIC} - r_d)\frac{D}{E}ROE=ROIC+(ROIC−rd​)ED​, where rdr_drd​ is the after-tax cost of debt.
(a) What is ROE?
(b) The company's cost of capital (weighted over debt and equity) is 8%. Management says: "Our ROE is far above 8%, so we are creating value for shareholders." What is wrong with this claim?
Question 3
A company has 45 days of receivables, 60 days of inventory and 30 days of payables. Annual revenue is 3650 (simplification: compute all three on revenue, so revenue is 10 a day).
(a) How many days is the cash conversion cycle?
(b) The company improves inventory management and cuts days of inventory to 40. Roughly how much cash is freed? How does this affect ROIC?
Question 4
A company has current assets of 500 (cash 50, receivables 150, inventory 300) and current liabilities of 400.
(a) What are its current ratio and quick ratio?
(b) Why does a high current ratio not necessarily mean strong short-term solvency? Why do some large retailers operate normally with a current ratio below 1?
